title: Search Insert Position
description: Brute force to optimized: a linear scan for the first qualifying index versus a binary search that finds it directly.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a sorted array of distinct integers nums and a target value, return the index of target if it is found. If not, return the index where it would be inserted to keep the array sorted.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: Find the first index in the sorted array whose value is greater than or equal to target. If target itself is present, that index is exactly where it is found; if not, it is exactly where target should be inserted.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding Where to Insert a New Book on an Alphabetized Shelf
blocks.text: Picture a shelf of books already sorted alphabetically, and needing to find exactly where a new book should slide in, or where an existing one already sits, without checking every book one by one.
2 is not present; it would be inserted at index 1, between 1 and 3.
Edge case: target is smaller than every element, or larger than every element
If target is smaller than nums[0], the answer is 0; if larger than every element, the answer is nums.length.
Before scanning left to right, notice the array's sorted order makes this exactly the kind of "find the first position satisfying a condition" problem binary search is built for.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The target index is always "the first position where nums[i] is at least target," whether or not target itself is actually present.

Observation 2: Since nums is sorted, this condition, nums[i] is at least target, is false for a prefix of indices and true for the rest, a single flip point.

Observation 3: Binary search finds that flip point directly, narrowing the range in half at every step instead of scanning linearly.

Observation 4: The search converges once the range narrows to a single index, which is exactly the answer.
This leads directly to a binary search for the first index where nums[i] is at least target.
Scan the array left to right, returning the first index whose value is at least target.

items: For every index i from 0 to n minus 1, check if nums[i] is at least target.
If none is found, return n (target belongs at the very end).

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: scan left to right for the first value at least target

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every index is checked in order, stopping at the first one satisfying the condition.
The sorted order of nums is never actually used to skip any comparisons.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), scanning up to the entire array.
Space: O(1).
Limitation: the array's sorted order guarantees the condition "nums[i] is at least target" flips at most once across the whole array, a fact the linear scan does not exploit.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why a linear scan wastes the sorted order: once nums[i] is at least target for some i, it remains true for every later i too, since the array is sorted, meaning a single binary search can find that flip point directly.

What the binary search narrows toward: the smallest index where nums[mid] is at least target, discarding the left half whenever nums[mid] is still too small.

The core idea: standard binary search for the first index satisfying a monotonic condition.

Binary search with lo starting at 0 and hi starting at nums.length. At each step, if nums[mid] is less than target, the answer must be to the right, so move lo past mid; otherwise, mid could be the answer, so keep it in range and move hi to mid. Stop when lo and hi meet.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: binary search for the first index at least target

blocks.text: Since nums is sorted, "nums[i] is at least target" is false for every index before some point and true from that point onward. Binary search narrows in on exactly that boundary, discarding half the remaining range at every step, and converges on the first qualifying index.

blocks.text: This problem is a direct introduction to binary searching for "the first index satisfying a condition," rather than only searching for an exact match, a pattern that generalizes to many other binary search problems.

items: Only handling the case where target is found, forgetting the array could need target inserted anywhere from index 0 to nums.length.
Using hi = nums.length minus 1 instead of nums.length, which can make it awkward to represent "insert at the very end."

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["target smaller than every element","Returns 0."],["target larger than every element","Returns nums.length."]]}

blocks.text: Framing the problem as "find the first index where nums[i] is at least target" up front, rather than treating found and not-found as separate cases, leads to a cleaner binary search.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "what if the target is not in the array", think: the answer is still just the first index where nums[i] is at least target.

Any "binary search for the boundary of a condition" problem, a very common binary search variant.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n) time; the optimized binary search runs in O(log n) time. Both use O(1) space.

items: Pattern: binary search for the first index satisfying a monotonic condition.
Core Idea: the insertion point is always the first index where nums[i] is at least target, found directly with binary search.
Time: O(n) for the brute force, O(log n) for the optimized binary search.
Most Important Observation: found and not-found cases do not need separate handling; both reduce to the same "first index at least target" search.
Interview Difficulty: a foundational binary search problem.
One line memory trick: binary search for the first index at least target.
